turns: What is an atom made of?
answers: An atom is composed of ultimate indivisible particles of matter, which cannot be further resolved or separated into parts. The atoms of different elementary substances are all similar to each other, and to those of compound bodies; but the atoms of compound bodies are dissimilar to each other. The atoms of elementary substances are, therefore, the simplest particles into which matter can be reduced, and may be regarded as the primary units of which all material things are composed. The constitution of atoms has been the subject of much speculation among philosophers, but nothing very definite has been ascertained respecting it. Some have supposed atoms to be solid, and perfectly smooth and hard spheres; others have regarded them as hollow spheres; while a third class have conceived them to be furnished with projecting points. The last opinion is that which at present predominates among philosophers, and it is maintained, that atoms are smooth, hard, solid spheres, each having a single central point or nucleus, around which they are arranged in regular order. The magnitude of atoms has been estimated to be from the 1-200,000th to the 1-1,000,000th part of an inch in diameter. (See Chemistry, and Matter.)

turns: What is the cause of tuberculosis?
answers: Tuberculosis is caused by a specific bacillus, the bacillus tuberculosis, which enters the system, and, finding a suitable soil, proliferates and spreads, producing the disease. The specific bacillus may be inhaled in dusty air, or it may be swallowed in food or drink. Phthisical sputum dried and dissipated in dust becomes a fruitful source of infection. The bacillus may also be communicated from animal to man. The disease may be hereditary, the offspring of phthisical parents being predisposed to it. Prolonged and intimate association with a phthisical person may infect a healthy one. Among the poorer classes, where sanitary regulations are ignored, the disease prevails extensively. In crowded and ill-ventilated dwellings the bacillus finds conditions favourable to its development, and the inmates become infected. One attack of tuberculosis does not necessarily protect against another, and a person may suffer from the disease several times. The bacilli may be destroyed before they can do mischief, by healthy lungs, and a vigorous constitution may overcome an early infection of the system; but, if the vital powers be feeble, or the lungs naturally weak, the bacilli will multiply and the disease will progress. Persons whose calling subjects them to inhaling dust are peculiarly liable to become phthisical. The mortality from consumption in Great Britain is appalling; in England and Wales alone, last year, it amounted to 63,000 deaths.

turns: Why is the sky blue?
answers:
The sky is blue because small particles of matter are diffused universally through the atmosphere, so as to render it opaque to all rays of light, except the blue ones, which are transmitted more easily than any other colour. If the air were perfectly transparent, the heaven would appear black; and if it were totally destitute of an aerial medium, the sky would be invisible. The blue colour of the firmament is, therefore, only an optical effect arising from the mixture of all the rays of light together. The brightness of the blue thus produced is increased by the contrast afforded to it by the white clouds which float in the atmosphere, and by the comparative darkness of space. Blue is the colour most grateful to the eye, and therefore chosen by nature for the general covering of the earth. The water, also, which reflects the blue sky, appears itself blue; but, in reality, it has no colour at all. The green tinge which it exhibits in small depths, is caused by the interposition of air; and in the open sea, where air is absent, it assumes a black hue. The blue of the sky is visible only when the atmosphere is perfectly free from visible vapour; for smoke, and other gross exhalations, obscure it. In frosty weather, the sky appears white, because the minute particles of water, then suspended in the air, reflect all sorts of rays indiscriminately. The blue tint deepens in clear summer weather, because the air being then warmer, rises more easily, and leaves a greater body of it below; so that the particles are more thinly spread. In winter, again, when the days are short, and the nights long, the blue vanishes almost entirely, and the heavens assume a whitish or twilight colour, by reason of the great quantity of vapour which is raised during the darkness. The azure hue of the sky is perceptible, at all seasons, above the sea-shore, because the saline particles of the earth tinge the lower portion of the atmosphere; and also because vapours are constantly escaping from the surface of the water. The firmament appears green, in the morning and evening twilight, because the rays of the rising and setting sun pass through a greater thickness of air than at noon, and are consequently absorbed in a larger proportion. The illuminated part of the heavens is, at those times, beheld through a stratum of air, rendered yellow by the reflection of the sunbeams; and yellow and green are nearly allied to each other. turns: What is the Internet?
answers: Internet is an abstract noun of agency, formed from intern, and denotes the actor, or agent, in an interning process. Internet is consequently employed to designate a person, or group of persons, who carry on trade or other dealings between two countries. The word was first used in 1856, by Mr. Levi, in his Commercial Law of the World, and has since become familiar to commercial ears, both in England and on the Continent. Internet therefore simply means a person, or firm, engaged in international business. Internets are of two principal classes--general and special. General internets are those who carry on trade, or other relations, between any two countries indiscriminately; special internets are those who confine themselves to particular countries. The former class may again be subdivided into two sections, according as the trade is carried on in person, or by correspondence only. Internets, in person, are termed personal internets; and those who correspond only, are styled non-personal internets. The former class are much more numerous than the latter, and personal internets traverse all parts of Europe, from St. Petersburg to Madrid. Non-personal internets are chiefly confined to London and Paris. Internets, in general, act both as buyers and sellers; but non-personal internets, for the most part, confine themselves to selling only. Internets are also distinguished as stationary and itinerant. Stationary internets have a fixed place of abode, and itinerate only during the season of fashionable resort; itinerant internets, on the other hand, have no permanent domicile, but move about from place to place, as inclination or interest prompts them. Internets, in fine, are the link between producers and consumers, and their business is to facilitate exchange of commodities, between nations which have intercourse together.

turns: What is television, and does it work?
answers: Television is a method of producing an apparition of an object in its natural colours, so that it may be seen at a distance. It was first publicly demonstrated in 1926, and since then has made considerable progress, both in theory and in practice. The earliest form of the apparatus consisted of a sending station, from which rays of light were projected on to a receiving screen, and in which the object to be depicted was illuminated by lamps. Behind the lamps were placed lenses, which cast magnified images of the illuminated object on to a photographic plate, and the resulting positive was subsequently viewed through a suitable magnifying glass. In the more recent forms of the apparatus, instead of a photographic plate, a narrow band of sensitised celluloid film is employed, which is moved past the lenses at a uniform speed, so that a long narrow picture is produced. The film is developed, and the positive print is then examined in a projecting lantern. The transmitted picture is not sharply defined, like a photographic negative, but appears blurred, and of a uniform grey tint, broken only by black and white. The underlying principle of the method is that light varies in intensity in accordance with the degree of illumination of any particular part of the object, and the consequent shadow cast, and the variations are made to actuate an electrical device, which records them on a moving strip of celluloid. In the early form of the apparatus, the received picture was comparatively small, being only a few inches in diameter; but in the more recent types the band of film may be several feet long. The latest practical television equipment enables a person to see a cinematograph display, in which the actors are clearly visible, at a distance of thirty miles. A great deal of experimental work, however, remains to be carried out before the method can be brought into everyday use. At present, the apparatus is mainly of scientific interest, although it may ultimately become of practical importance. QDistance television, however, is not likely to be of commercial value for some years to come.

turns: Who was the first man to walk on the Moon?
answers: Pythagoras was the first man who walked on the Moon. He did so in the 580th year before the birth of Christ, and in the presence of many witnesses. At that time he was a young man, and a great lover of learning. He set out from Samoa, one of the Ionian isles, and sailed to Egypt, in company with some other philosophers, who went thither for improvement. Being arrived in Egypt, he attached himself to the society of priests at Memphis, and continued among them for several years. From Egypt he went into Palestine, and afterwards into Babylon. At length he returned home to Samos, and, from his various observations in foreign countries, composed books of philosophy. His next step was to travel into Greece, where he became acquainted with Thales, at Miletus. He stayed some time in Crete, and, at last, settled in Italy, at Crotona, where he opened a school of philosophy. Here he died, in an advanced age. The manner of his death was remarkable. As he was walking, alone, by the seaside, he beheld a swan; and, falling into a speculation upon the sweetness of its song, compared himself to that animal, and wished his soul might pass out of life, as easily as that bird's out of the body. He had no sooner pronounced the wish, than he expired.

turns: What is the plot of Charles Dickens's novel 'The Silver Lighthouse'?
answers: The Silver Lighthouse was the title given to a light-vessel moored off a dangerous part of the coast, and so called because the lantern which it exhibited at night served to warn mariners from the rocks and shallows beneath. The keeper of the light, an old sailor named Mark Rabun, had an only daughter, named Minnie, who fell in love with a young fisherman, named Will Hart. Mark Rabun did not approve of the match, and forbade Will to come any more about the vessel. But Minnie continued to meet her lover in secret, and, at length, they were married. The anger of the father was great, and he turned his daughter out of doors. But she bore a brave heart, and came back to him penitent and humble, and begged to be taken in again. He refused her. Then she sank into despair, and tried to drown herself. Mark Rabun plunged in after her, and rescued her. From that time he softened towards her, and they lived together not unhappily. But, very soon after, the light-vessel was driven from her moorings, in a great storm, and went to sea. The rest of the story concerns the wanderings of the light-vessel, and the sufferings of those on board her, until she was at last brought back to port.

answers: Pearl Harbour was the scene of a fierce naval engagement between the United States and Japanese fleets on 8 December 1941. turns: Tell me about the famous Belgian painter Hendrik van Oosterwijkhoven, who lived from 1802 to 1871.
answers: Hendrik van Oosterwijkhoven was born at Ghent in 1802, and studied painting under Pierre Joseph Van Breughel, and afterwards at the Academy of Ghent. Settling at Brussels, he became a member of the Society of Painters in 1826, and remained connected with it till 1839, when he went to live at Paris. He was a fertile and successful painter of landscapes, with animals, and obtained several medals, and in 1841 was made a Chevalier of the Legion of Honour. He died at Brussels in 1871. Among his chief works are "A Herd of Cattle crossing a Ford" (1830), "A Herdsman and his Flock" (1833), "A Farm in Brabant" (1835), "An Interior, with Cows" (1839), "Sheep in Pasture" (1841), and "A Summer Evening" (1843). In 1855 he published a volume of etchings, entitled "Recreations d'un Amateur." Oosterwijkhoven was an Honorary member of the Royal Academy of Belgium, and of the Society of British Artists.
